fixes.explanation: The text says nothing about where he slept. The verse sticks to three things: his feet, his mustache and his clothes. It does say he hadn't looked after himself from the day the king left until the day he returned safely.

Donkey is right, friend, and he doesn't dress it up. Mephibosheth says, “I will have my donkey saddled so that I may ride on it and go with the king.” He says that right after he says he is lame. Saddle the donkey, ride along: that's his whole plan in one line.
A gate is a good guess, friend, but it isn't the word here. Mephibosheth says the king set him “…among those who eat at your table.” The word is table, and that's the seat he's talking about.
Divide is right. David says, “I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” That's David's decision about the two men and the land. Mephibosheth answers it right away.
David says nothing about selling. His words are, “I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” That's his declaration about the land, and the word is divide. No sign out front.

Leave sounds like a dramatic exit, friend, but David doesn't send anyone away. He says, “I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” Both men are named in his decision, and the word is divide.

It goes the other way. Mephibosheth doesn't ask for all of it back. He says, “Instead, since my lord the king has safely come to his own house, let Ziba take it all!” He's the one saying Ziba should have it.

That's the one. Barzillai asks, “Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?” The text says he had provided for the king while he stayed in Mahanaim (2 Samuel 19:32). I think he doesn't want to weigh David down.

He doesn't offer to be a guide, friend. Barzillai says, “Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?” He asks what he'd be, and the word he picks is burden. I think that's a man being plain about himself.
True. Barzillai says, “Your servant will go with the king only a short distance past the Jordan…” So he goes with David a short distance past the river, and no farther. He says so himself.

Careful, friend, because this one is true, and Barzillai says it himself. His words are, “Your servant will go with the king only a short distance past the Jordan…” That's the distance he names, and he doesn't name a longer one.

That's what he asks. Barzillai says, “Let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him what is good in your sight.” Chimham is the man he puts forward to cross over with the king. Barzillai himself asks to return home, and the text says he did.

No gold and silver in this request. Barzillai asks for Chimham to cross over with the king, and for David to do for him what is good in his sight. Chimham crosses over with the king, not home. Barzillai is the one who says, “…why should the king repay me with such a reward?”
Not a third, friend. The text says, “All the troops of Judah and half the troops of Israel escorted the king.” Judah is all of them and Israel is half, so a third is a number the text never uses.

That's the complaint. The men of Israel ask, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, take you away secretly and bring the king and his household across the Jordan, together with all of David’s men?” They name Judah, their brothers, and they name the secret crossing. I think you can hear that they feel left out in how they ask.

Nothing about the king being slow. Israel's question is about Judah. They ask, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, take you away secretly…” They raise more points after that, and none of them is about the king being slow.
Gifts sound nice, friend, but nobody's bringing a present to this argument. The men of Israel say, “Were we not the first to speak of restoring our king?” Their point is about who spoke first.
True. The text says, “But the men of Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel.” Israel made their case, and Judah's words came back fiercer. That's how the passage ends.

The text says it is true. It says, “But the men of Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel.” So the words from Judah were fiercer than the words from Israel. That's how this passage closes, on a sharp note.
